title: Building full virtual vehicles on Google Cloud: From AAOS to the smallest MCU
raw_text: Imagining traditional gearheads getting their hands on software-defined vehicles is an amusing thought experiment. With their socket wrenches and air compressors at the ready, they might be confused to encounter core functions more likely to run on 1s and 0s than oil and belts. But across the auto industry these days, more and more vehicles feature prominent systems built using cloud-native development, continuous integration/continuous delivery, fast digital iteration, and plenty of AI. But there’s still a big gap to be found in many automakers’ and Tier 1 suppliers’ cloud-based development processes. On the one hand, these companies are commonly using software to develop vehicles’ digital entertainment and information screens, or other onboard high-performance computers. On the other, the dozens of microchips and control modules that make a car a car these days — such as gateways, body controllers, zone control units, sensor and actuator nodes — are still frequently hardwired to physical chips when they’re constructed, making them very difficult to update, reprogram, or expand after the vehicle drives off the factory floor. Teams have to wait for benches, samples, and rigs, and integration can easily slip to the end of the development process, where defects are most expensive to fix. This inherent inefficiency has become a leading bottleneck. After all, manufacturers can’t really claim vehicles are software-defined if most of their electronics only function when connected to physical hardware and if developers are leaning heavily on actual hardware. With Horizon, our agentic innovation platform for developing software-defined vehicles, our vision is to help manufacturers avoid these inefficiencies by working with partners like RemotiveLabs . The cockpit already runs in the cloud The Android team has invested a significant amount of time and effort over the last few years on enabling seamless development of the many digital systems in vehicles’ cockpits. Android Automotive OS (AAOS) runs inside Google’s official virtual testing environment for Android, Cuttlefish , which itself runs comfortably on Arm-based Google Cloud instances . With this approach, developers can build, boot, and test virtual versions of their infotainment stacks on the same Arm architecture that ships in vehicles. And with the recent launch of Android 17 and AAOS SDV , this capability is also extended to further domains, whenever AAOS SDV is used. Deploying it with Cuttlefish, for example, proves the model: representative software, on representative architecture, in the cloud, on demand. The question that still needs to be answered is how to extend that model to the rest of the vehicle, especially when other operating systems are involved. The harness around the virtual vehicle That’s where RemotiveTopology comes into play. As the harness around the virtual vehicle, it’s the layer that connects AAOS in Cuttlefish to a full, simulated electrical and electronic (E/E) architecture: the rest of the vehicle’s onboard computers, its data networks, and the live signals that make the system function like a real vehicle rather than a collection of standalone apps. RemotiveTopology automatically utilizes manufacturers’ existing network design files to build a working, virtual version of their cars’ networks. This is vehicle-as-code: the E/E architecture expressed as an executable specification, versioned and provisioned like infrastructure-as-code. In this way, an entire vehicle can be spun up on demand. Cockpit software talks to the rest of the vehicle exactly as it would in a real vehicle. As a result, developers get full and continuous signal and cross-domain visibility, so they can see real-time system status. And because it is built on standard Linux tooling, the same topology runs on a laptop and in a contiguous integration pipeline on Google Cloud. Integrate across domains early, not late The payoff for using this approach is that all onboard systems can be developed and integrated with software before any of them are connected to a vehicle’s hardware. That’s beneficial because the most difficult (and latest) integration in a vehicle’s development is bringing all its systems together. For example, advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) produce object lists, trajectories, and mode requests that the cockpit has to render and react to, while the infotainment system and information cluster have to reflect driving state while body and chassis nodes sit in the loop. With the full topology live on Google Cloud, the infotainment system and ADAS can operate simultaneously within a virtual vehicle, exchanging real signals over the simulated network. This means it’s possible to exercise handoffs like an ADAS event surfacing in the cluster or a driver-mode change rippling across domains from day one in continuous integration long before the benches and samples line up. In this way, developers can be confident they’ll discover multi-domain integration long before the end of the process so that they can test continuously from the start. The full vehicle frontier At the heart of this work is a shared desire to bring scalable software development to even the smallest and most common nodes in a vehicle, its microchips and control modules. That’s because these are the parts that have traditionally been wired to hardware, and as a result are the biggest blocker to fully software-defined vehicles. The ultimate goal is that the same software that runs in the cloud can run on vehicles’ actual control modules with no re-tooling or re-validation needed to move between them. That parity is natural with Arm-based Google Cloud infrastructure because the cloud and the car share an instruction set. Google's Axion makes it straightforward: C4A metal, a bare-metal Arm instance , is provided explicitly for automotive systems development and Android software development, giving direct hardware access without unnecessary software layers and delivering the consistent performance that vehicle systems require. Taken together, this holistic system allows teams, for the first time, to develop and integration-test an entire vehicle’s systems in the cloud and then apply it to the actual vehicle without having to rewrite it. Why now, and where to start The payoff is not abstract. Treating the vehicle as code and moving integration into the cloud compresses the slowest, most expensive phase of a program. Early customer engagements with RemotiveLabs have measured more than 10x faster integration cycles. And the development loop is now changing faster than the hardware loop: AI-assisted and agentic workflows can rapidly generate, test, and refine vehicle software, but only virtual systems provide the required scale. Every element that can’t be virtualized can slow the entire development process down. RemotiveTopology provides this architecture as vehicle-as-code and makes it accessible for developers, testers, and autonomous AI agents alike. Best of all, there is no new third-party tooling to adopt just to get started. Instead, RemotiveLabs publishes an open-source simplified vehicle on GitHub that anyone can run in minutes on standard Linux tooling and platform definitions already in place. Full existing toolchains plug in as a manufacturer or Tier1 supplier scales, and RemotiveTopology can be easily dropped into an Arm-based Google Cloud environment. For those building software-defined vehicles whose virtual development stops at the cockpit, it’s time to start with an open-source example, bring unique platform definitions, and run an entire vehicle in the cloud. RemotiveTopology is available in Horizon for easy usage in combination with other Horizon modules.

title: How to Use Python UDF Logging for Pipeline Observability
raw_text:
We are announcing a new logging feature that is now available in Python User-Defined Function (UDF) in BigQuery. Developers can now use Python’s standard logging library directly inside BigQuery UDFs to emit structured logs seamlessly into Cloud Logging—with zero external plugins or custom connectors required. While UDF logging enables a wide range of operational monitoring and debugging workflows, to demonstrate this feature we are showcasing an example for building fault-tolerant, resilient data pipelines. In the example below, we are capturing row-level diagnostic telemetry during query execution, so that teams can easily isolate problematic records, trigger real-time alerts, and triage issues via SQL without halting entire workloads. In this post, we’ll show you how to get started with Python UDF logging and walk through an e-commerce event ingestion pipeline as a practical, end-to-end example. Architecture overview The workflow consists of three stages: Inline validation : The Python UDF parses incoming JSON payloads. Valid records pass to the destination table; corrupted or non-compliant rows trigger logging.error() and return NULL to prevent query failure. Real-time alerting : A Cloud Monitoring log-based metric notifies your team when error rates breach SLA thresholds. SQL triage & replay : Data engineers query the quarantined payloads in BigQuery using standard SQL over the linked _AllLogs view, diagnose the root cause, and re-ingest recovered data. Although this specific demonstration relies on Python for data validation and transformation, you can seamlessly integrate Python-driven logging and validation into pipelines that perform SQL-based transformations. Quickstart walkthrough: Step-by-step Step 1: Create the generic Python UDF This UDF parses JSON and checks for a required field. If parsing fails or the required key is missing, it logs structured diagnostic JSON and returns NULL . code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION `YOUR_PROJECT.YOUR_DATASET.safe_parse_json`(
 raw_payload STRING,
 required_key STRING
)
RETURNS STRING
LANGUAGE python
OPTIONS (entry_point='safe_parse_json', runtime_version='python-3.11')
AS r'''
import json
import logging

def safe_parse_json(raw_payload, required_key):
 if not raw_payload or raw_payload.strip() == "":
 logging.warning(json.dumps({"error_type": "EMPTY_PAYLOAD"}))
 return None

 try:
 data = json.loads(raw_payload)
 if required_key and (required_key not in data or data[required_key] is None):
 logging.error(json.dumps({
 "error_type": "MISSING_REQUIRED_KEY",
 "missing_key": required_key,
 "raw_payload": raw_payload[:200]
 }))
 return None
 return json.dumps(data)

 except Exception as e:
 logging.error(json.dumps({
 "error_type": "JSON_SYNTAX_ERROR",
 "error_message": str(e),
 "raw_payload": raw_payload[:200]
 }))
 return None
''';'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9be51eca10>)])]> Step 2: Run ingestion with logging enabled In this example, we simulate an e-commerce event ingestion pipeline processing incoming user actions ( click , view , checkout ). Our goal is to extract valid events into our clean analytics table while gracefully quarantining broken or missing-schema payloads. Enable logging in your session with SET @@udf.properties : code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'SET @@udf.properties = JSON '{"enableDebugOutput": true}';

CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE `YOUR_PROJECT.YOUR_DATASET.clean_events` AS
WITH sample_events AS (
 SELECT 'evt_001' AS event_id, '{"user_id": "usr_101", "event": "click", "amount": 25.5}' AS raw_data UNION ALL
 SELECT 'evt_002' AS event_id, 'corrupted_json{' AS raw_data UNION ALL -- Syntax error
 SELECT 'evt_003' AS event_id, '{"event": "view"}' AS raw_data UNION ALL -- Missing required user_id
 SELECT 'evt_004' AS event_id, '{"user_id": "usr_102", "event": "checkout", "amount": 99.0}' AS raw_data
),
parsed_events AS (
 SELECT
 event_id,
 `YOUR_PROJECT.YOUR_DATASET.safe_parse_json`(raw_data, 'user_id') AS validated_json
 FROM sample_events
)
SELECT
 event_id,
 JSON_VALUE(validated_json, '$.user_id') AS user_id,
 JSON_VALUE(validated_json, '$.event') AS event_name,
 'VALID' AS status
FROM parsed_events
WHERE validated_json IS NOT NULL;'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f9be51ee050>)])]> Ingestion Results event_id user_id event_name status evt_001 usr_101 click VALID evt_004 usr_102 checkout VALID The query succeeds without interruption while bad rows (2 and 3) are routed to Cloud Logging. Step 3: Set up real-time alerts on Cloud Logging You can configure alerts to notify your on-call team as soon as malformed payloads exceed acceptable thresholds. In the Google Cloud Console (1-Click) In the Google Cloud Console, open Logs Explorer . Paste the log filter for your UDF routine: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'resource.type="bigquery.googleapis.com/ManagedRoutineInvocation"

Step 4: Triage bad rows with BigQuery Log Analytics "Note: To query your logs via BigQuery SQL, ensure you have enabled BigQuery Log Analytics on your Cloud Logging bucket and created a linked dataset." Replay and recover quarantined rows from Cloud Logging sink table
INSERT INTO `YOUR_PROJECT.YOUR_DATASET.clean_events` (event_id, user_id, event_name, status)
SELECT
 'evt_003_recovered' AS event_id,

Other use cases Shadow execution & safe migrations : Run legacy and new business logic side-by-side in a UDF. Return the legacy result to production while logging calculation differences to Cloud Logging. PII redaction auditing : Mask sensitive tokens (such as SSNs or account numbers) before writing to BigQuery, while emitting anonymized audit events to Cloud Logging. ML inference drift : Log warnings when embedded scoring logic encounters out-of-vocabulary inputs or low model confidence. Best practices Enable debug output : Include SET @@udf.properties = JSON '{"enableDebugOutput": true}'; in the session where you want logs captured. Avoid sensitive data in logs : Cloud Logging is visible to users with Logging Viewer permissions. Do not log credentials or secrets. Cost management : On high-throughput pipelines, log selectively (e.g., only on errors or via sampling) to manage logging ingestion volume. title: Developer’s guide to implementing MCP apps in Gemini
raw_text: Enterprise assistants still respond mostly in text. However, that can break down for visual, multi-step work, where every adjustment costs another slow chat turn. MCP Apps ( SEP-1865 ) solves this. This open Model Context Protocol (MCP) extension pairs a tool with a live UI. In Gemini Enterprise , that UI renders directly in the chat flow inside a sandboxed iframe, and can expand to fullscreen or a side panel. Edits run locally while the workspace and assistant stay synchronized. You also avoid rebuilding core foundations: Gemini provides workforce sign-in, governed data access, and the Default Assistant, while you host your MCP server on a private Cloud Run service. Why we need MCP Apps Enterprise assistants have evolved through three generations: Generation 1 (Text chatbots): Returns static markdown with no interactive controls. Generation 2 (Standard MCP tools): Invokes live APIs, but outputs static text. Every change requires another model turn. Generation 3 (Interactive MCP Apps): Pairs each tool with a live workspace. Adjustments happen in the widget without a model turn, while the assistant stays in sync. Building MCP Apps in Gemini delivers six benefits: Responsive user experience: Single-click actions execute directly in the panel without round-tripping through the chat. Purpose-built workflows: Deliver visual redaction views for legal review, 3D viewers for CAD, or sensitivity models for finance. Enterprise security: Workforce OAuth sign-in, private Cloud Run ingress, and a sandboxed iframe protect every layer. Human-in-the-loop governance: Experts inspect and approve high-stakes actions before execution. Open standard: Portable across compatible hosts, with automatic text fallback. Broad connectivity: Connect to BigQuery, Agent Platform, Cloud Storage, or internal ERP and CRM systems. High-level architecture Three decoupled tiers work together: Client browser: Shows the chat alongside the MCP App widget in the side panel. Gemini Enterprise: The default assistant calls tools, the AppBridge proxy relays widget messages, and the connector manages OAuth. Google Cloud (your project): You deploy and host the MCP server on Cloud Run, which exposes one JSON-RPC endpoint (/mcp), runs background jobs, and serves the single-file HTML widget. Each tier talks only to its neighbor, letting Gemini Enterprise enforce security and routing. Authentication with two independent layers Each user signs in through OAuth 2.0. On every call, Gemini Enterprise sends its service agent token alongside the user's OAuth token: Layer 1 (Cloud Run IAM): Enforced at Google's edge, this answers "which service may call?" Public access is disabled; unauthorized callers receive HTTP 403 . Layer 2 (In-App OAuth): Enforced inside the application, this answers "which user is calling?" Failed verification returns HTTP 401 , prompting the user to sign in again. Cloud Run IAM cannot distinguish end users, so both layers are required. Outbound calls use a least-privilege service account. Build, deploy on Google Cloud, and register in Gemini Enterprise First, build your custom MCP server (exposing POST /mcp and a bundled ui:// HTML widget) using the MCP Apps SDK , or use Google Antigravity to scaffold and deploy your MCP App with this starter prompt: Build an MCP App for Gemini Enterprise using the create-mcp-app skill (https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/tree/main/plugins/mcp-apps/skills/create-mcp-app). Workflow: [describe your input data, side-panel UI controls, and approval or export actions]. Generate a single-file HTML widget, a Streamable HTTP backend (POST /mcp) with <2s async tool responses and get_app_state polling, and Cloud Run deployment commands (--no-allow-unauthenticated, --no-cpu-throttling, --min-instances=1). Once your MCP server code is ready, deploy it to Cloud Run and connect it to Gemini Enterprise : Step 1: Enable APIs for Cloud Run, Discovery Engine, Agent Platform, and Organization Policy. Step 2: Deploy your MCP server container to Cloud Run from source (gcloud run deploy <service> --source . ) with --no-allow-unauthenticated, --no-cpu-throttling so background work does not freeze between polls, and --min-instances=1 . Step 3: Grant the invoker role ( roles/run.invoker ) to your Discovery Engine service agent (Layer 1). Step 4: Create an OAuth 2.0 Web Client with redirect URI https://vertexaisearch.cloud.google.com/oauth-redirect (Layer 2). Step 5: Override the discoveryengine.managed.disableCustomMcpServerConnector constraint and complete the Before you begin prerequisites (roles/discoveryengine.editor for the admin, allowedEgressFqdns for your server and OAuth hosts, and custom_mcp in allowedDataSources if enforced). Then, in the Google Cloud Console under Gemini Enterprise > Data stores > Create data store, select Custom MCP Server and register the connector: Configuration field Value MCP Server URL https://<your-cloud-run-service>.run.app/mcp Authorization URL https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth Token URL https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token Client ID and Secret Your Web OAuth 2.0 Client ID and Secret Scopes openid email profile Enable PKCE Support Checked (recommended) Use HTTP Basic Auth Unchecked (avoids invalid_client errors) Step 6: Enable actions on your data store. Gemini Enterprise imports your MCP server's tools as actions and disables them by default. In the Cloud Console, open Gemini Enterprise > Data stores > [Your MCP Data Store] > Actions, click Reload custom actions (which calls tools/list on your server), select your model-visible tools, and click Enable actions. Step 7: Connect the data store to your app . Open Gemini Enterprise > Apps > [Your App] > Connected data stores > Add existing data stores , and select your MCP data store. Connecting it as a data store gives the built-in Default Assistant access to your MCP tools and UI widget directly in main chat ( do not use "Add Agent," which is for external sub-agents rather than MCP data stores). Build your own An MCP App pairs backend tools with a live workspace in Gemini Enterprise. You do not build a chat frontend or identity pipeline; you deploy one Cloud Run container and attach it as a Data Store, making Gemini Enterprise where enterprise work gets done. Try Gemini here Co-build with Google Antigravity here Build on Google Cloud: MCP Apps Specification (SEP-1865) , Cloud Run , and Google Cloud AI .

title: Who judges the judge? Three helpful ways to audit your LLM evaluators
raw_text: Is your LLM-as-a-judge truly objective? There’s a common misconception in tech that humans are subjective, so we should rely on AI for objective evaluation. But the reality is that LLMs are also subjective. Just like human reviewers, they can carry biases: Verbosity bias : LLM judges usually favor longer, confident-sounding answers , even when the underlying facts are wrong. Position bias : Swapping the order of two options can cause an LLM judge to flip its verdict over 75% of the time . The halo effect : Because LLMs generate text piece by piece, clean grammar and formatting can trick an AI judge into giving top marks for accuracy while missing errors. Agreeableness bias : LLM judges are great at recognizing valid work. But with detecting errors, they may fail to catch incorrect, buggy, or unsafe outputs up to 75% of the time . Self-enhancement bias: Also known as egocentric bias, AI evaluators systematically overrate outputs that were generated by themselves or from their own family. Ultimately, LLM judges are not objective arbiters of truth. They are subjective models with their own distinct biases. Treating them as infallible tools that don't need their quality measured might leave your work compromised. In this post, we’ll explore what’s holding enterprises back from strong evals, and share an easy three-pillar method you can use to improve your quality. Three helpful ways to audit your LLM judges Pillar 1: Measure internal stability Before you can trust an AI judge’s score, you need to know that it isn't just guessing. Because LLMs are probabilistic, they can be inconsistent, giving different scores to the exact same text. You can test this internal stability by running multi-pass consistency checks on a single output and calculating the variance. If a judge's scores fluctuate wildly on identical inputs, its rubric is too ambiguous. Pillar 2: Validate human alignment When your evaluation datasets are mostly valid responses, a lenient AI judge can look great on paper. It might align closely with human reviewers overall, but miss a majority of invalid or even unsafe outputs. To prove your LLM judge is catching real errors, you need chance-corrected metrics. These mathematical models filter out agreements driven purely by leniency or random chance, showing how closely your evaluator actually aligns with the informed decisions of human experts. Pillar 3: Use multi-judge ensembles To avoid the halo effect mentioned earlier, teams should use decomposed prompting. Instead of asking one LLM judge to score an entire response, assign a specialized judge to evaluate a single criteria, like factual accuracy or tone. This isolates traits and forces independent scoring. Second, to track performance in real time without human intervention, the established best practice is ensembling. This means running at least two different models under the hood to evaluate the exact same output simultaneously. By finding the statistical consensus between these models, you can flag if their evaluations begin to diverge and avoid any scoring quality degradation.
