By morning, staff were filling skips with meat, frozen goods and vegetables. Coopérative U counted 80 affected stores out of roughly 2,000.

title: OT systems complicate quantum-resistant data protection
raw_text: Quantum-resistant cryptography presents security leaders with various challenges, but CISOs in industries dependent on IoT and operational technology (OT) devices may face a particularly difficult journey to quantum readiness, especially if sensitive information that must remain confidential for years passes through those devices. A recent report from cybersecurity firm Forescout highlights these challenges in the healthcare industry, where medical histories, diagnostic images, and laboratory results, which retain their sensitivity long after they are created, routinely get transferred between various operational systems. Attackers who collect encrypted traffic carrying this information today can store it for decryption when sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available, an approach security experts call “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL). “PQC [post-quantum cryptography] migration in healthcare is not just about data confidentiality, but also patient safety,” the Forescout researchers say in their report, which examined over 2.5 million devices across more than 50 organizations. “Cryptography protects commands sent to medical devices, telemetry received from those devices for diagnostic purposes, medication orders, and other sensitive interactions. Quantum threats include unauthorized remote access by exploiting public keys for authentication, tampering with device-to-device communication by decrypting traffic, and sophisticated malware exploiting firmware integrity signatures.” While upgrading to PQC is relatively straightforward for live servers, where a standardized PQC algorithm can be implemented as a library package upgrade and configuration change, embedded devices such as those used in healthcare need full firmware updates from their manufacturers. Moreover, those upgrades must maintain backwards compatibility with other systems that might not be upgraded at the same time, and in the case of certified devices, they might require re-certification. This issue goes beyond healthcare to include industrial installations or anywhere OT or IoT devices handle sensitive or business-critical data. Last month, the G7 Cybersecurity Working Group urged governments and organizations to begin migrating to PQC as soon as possible, calling for action across all sectors. The group warned that the transition will be lengthy and that organizations should prepare before quantum computers capable of breaking current cryptography become available. Daniel dos Santos, VP of research at Forescout, tells CSO that while government bodies have issued orders and advisories with different expectations for PQC readiness, they all tend to converge on a 2030 timeline, which is when experts expect quantum computers might be capable of breaking existing encryption algorithms. For industries such as healthcare, however, the HNDL threat collapses that quantum-readiness timeline completely. Patient data travels beyond the medical device Protecting patient information requires securing the entire communication chain, from the equipment that generates the data to the IT systems that store it and the applications that make it available to doctors and patients. That includes, for example, a CT scanner that sends images to a picture archiving and communication system (PACS), images that can later be transferred between hospitals, cloud services, and external radiology providers, requiring quantum-resistant protection on each transfer to maintain long-term confidentiality. Laboratory results and prescription records follow similar routes. Electronic prescribing services exchange medication information between providers and pharmacies, including records of controlled substances and treatment for chronic diseases. Attackers can potentially intercept and siphon that data at different points in the chain: at the device level, from an internal network, through a compromised edge router or firewall, or even at the telecom operator’s level . The platforms that store and exchange patient records are often accessible directly from the internet as well. In a Shodan search, Forescout identified more than 5,500 internet-exposed instances of medical information systems, with electronic medical record platforms accounting for 46% of those instances and PACS accounting for 40%. Only 36% of PACS, 33% of electronic medical record systems, and 13% of laboratory information management systems had support for TLS 1.3, the only version of the protocol that supports ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism), a quantum-resistant key encapsulation standard published by NIST. However, the presence of TLS 1.3 does not demonstrate that a connection uses quantum-resistant cryptography, because the connecting client might negotiate a different algorithm. Furthermore, in a previous study published in June , Forescout found that only 11.8% of SSH servers on the internet are PQC-capable, a number that falls to 3% when looking only at Dropbear, an SSH server commonly used on embedded devices. Inside enterprise networks, 50% of IT devices use OpenSSH versions that support PQC, but only 28% of IoT, 16% of OT, and 6% of IoMT devices use the same versions. “Specialized devices are unlikely to be fully migrated this decade if we keep going at the current pace, delaying broader PQC migration efforts and quantum readiness,” the researchers concluded. “Unfortunately, medical devices are among those with the lowest adoption rates and the hardest challenges for adopting PQC.” Challenges extend beyond healthcare Changing cryptography on equipment used for patient care or industrial operations is completely dependent on the device vendor. Dos Santos says modifying the device filesystem independently, even when it can be done, jeopardizes certification, maintenance, and support, and any communication protocol changes need to preserve connections to other equipment. The same problem exists for devices in chemical plants, electricity networks, water treatment facilities, and factory floors. Some medical and industrial equipment already runs on Linux, which could in theory make adopting PQC easier, dos Santos says. However, he has seen little discussion of PQC adoption or roadmaps among OT vendors. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) described in its October 2024 OT guidance how changes to equipment controlling heavy machinery or combustible materials can require extensive safety testing. For medical devices, the regulatory implications depend on the changes made to the device. The US Food and Drug Administration’s February 2026 cybersecurity guidance says changes to authentication or encryption algorithms may require a new premarket submission. Concerns about legacy equipment and PQC extend across sectors. In a Certes survey of 200 IT and security professionals engaged with quantum-related risks at large US and UK organizations published in May, 78% of respondents rated the potential quantum threat to legacy environments as very high. For edge and IoT equipment, including industrial and medical devices, ATMs, and vehicles, 43% rated the threat as very high and another 31% as significant. Some devices will need alternative solutions Healthcare information, financial records, and trade secrets, such as code and industrial designs, can remain sensitive years after transmission. But not all data exchanged between devices has the same confidentiality requirements or operational relevance over time. “What’s missing from the policy conversation is a differentiated threat and risk assessment framework — one that accounts for data lifetime and sensitivity decay rate, device class, computational constraints, and realistic adversary capability timelines,” Sharon Hagi, CSO at IoT cybersecurity firm Finite State, told CSO in June after France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, outlined plans to introduce PQC requirements for product qualification starting in 2027. “The quantum threat is not uniformly distributed across the cryptographic stack,” Hagi said. “Shor’s algorithm breaks RSA and ECC. It does not break AES-256 or SHA-3 in any operationally practical sense — Grover’s provides at most a quadratic speedup, and the effective security margins of properly sized symmetric primitives still holds for most uses. Architectures that rely on symmetric encryption with out-of-band or pre-provisioned key distribution remain meaningful options for resource-constrained embedded devices where NIST PQC algorithms (e.g. ML-KEM, ML-DSA) impose non-trivial compute, bandwidth, and memory costs.” This means vendors will have to weigh carefully on which devices it’s even viable due to hardware limitations to deploy new PQC algorithms. In some cases, end-users might have to come up with alternatives, such as isolating those devices and routing traffic to and from them through other gateway devices that can apply PQC. This is the approach that users should start taking before vendors decide to release firmware upgrades, dos Santos says. For example, internet-facing websites and portals should already be configured to use TLS 1.3 as all modern browsers support it. For remote management and file transfers over the internet, deploy gateways that support protocols with quantum-resistant cryptography. A hospital could use a gateway to protect an image transfer to an external radiology provider. The hospital would still need to assess the connection from the scanner or image archive to that gateway and maybe isolate them on their own network segment with no direct internet access. “But at least for the external part, you’re reducing risk, right?” dos Santos says. But PQC support at one endpoint is effective only if the other endpoint can also negotiate the same algorithm, and manufacturers are reporting difficulty meeting interoperability goals. Thales’s September Manufacturing Data Threat Report , based on 417 respondents in 20 countries, revealed that 30% were behind on their post-quantum interoperability objectives. “For the end users, the main thing to be doing right now is the inventory of devices and data together,” dos Santos said. “Devices, data, and communication.” The resulting map should identify which transfers already have compatible protection, which depend on an upgrade, and where a gateway could protect an external connection. For healthcare, Forescout recommends prioritizing patient portals, external APIs, partner exchanges, and other internet-facing connections, then updating cryptographic libraries and firmware where feasible. For equipment that cannot be upgraded, its healthcare report recommends assessing gateways and isolation measures, obtaining vendor roadmaps, and planning replacement when manufacturers have no viable migration path. Dos Santos says vendors supplying equipment with multiyear service should have a roadmap for PQC communications even when their current firmware does not support it. Operators need to know when that support will arrive, which connections it will protect, and whether it requires new hardware. For equipment expected to remain in service for years, those answers need to inform purchasing and support agreements, alongside a replacement plan if a vendor cannot deliver an upgrade. The G7 call to action urges organizations to integrate quantum-safe replacements into normal equipment renewal schedules and the US Office of Management and Budget’s June guidance directs federal agencies to incorporate PQC upgrades into hardware refreshes and prioritize replacing or decommissioning equipment that cannot support PQC or hybrid cryptography.
summary: Quantum-resistant cryptography presents security leaders with various challenges, but CISOs in industries dependent on IoT and operational technology (OT) devices may face a particularly difficult journey to quantum readiness, especially if sensitive information that must remain confidential for years passes through those devices. A recent report from cybersecurity firm Forescout highlights these challenges in the healthcare industry, where medical histories, diagnostic images, and laboratory results, which retain their sensitivity long after they are created, routinely get transferred between various operational systems. Attackers who collect encrypted traffic carrying this information today can store it for decryption when sufficiently powerful quantum computers become available, an approach security experts call “harvest now, decrypt later” (HNDL). “PQC [post-quantum cryptography] migration in healthcare is not just about data confidentiality, but also patient safety,” the Forescout researchers say in their report, which examined over 2.5 million devices across more than 50 organizations.

title: F5 rushes out emergency NGINX patches for three critical flaws
raw_text: F5 is once again disclosing cybersecurity flaws in its core offerings. The app delivery and security provider has released out-of-band (OOB) security patches that address multiple flaws in NGINX, its high-performance software that controls digital traffic for websites. These include three critical-severity flaws that could allow attackers to crash systems, execute code, and launch denial of service (DoS) attacks. OOB security patches are emergency software updates released outside of normal maintenance cycles. CVE-2026-15176 , CVE-2026-97205 , and CVE-2026-93479 are rated 9.2 in severity in the latest version (4.0) of the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Impacted software products include NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source, NGINX Ingress Controller, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and NGINX Instance Manager. While F5 says it hasn’t discovered evidence that these issues are being exploited in the wild, it advises customers to install or upgrade to fixed versions. Analysts agree. “NGINX is the front door: Reverse proxy, load balancer, and Kubernetes ingress,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, noting that transport layer security (TLS) usually terminates in NGINX. “Code execution on that box means seeing passwords, session cookies, and API tokens in the clear, plus the private keys that make it all trustworthy.” Allowing attackers to crash systems CVE-2026-15176 and CVE-2026-97205 are ngx_http_core_module vulnerabilities in F5’s NGINX, which could cause a heap buffer overflow in the server’s worker process. This type of memory corruption could lead to a system crashing or restarting, thus giving attackers access. Threat actors could also execute code on systems where Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a technique intended to prevent exploitation by randomly arranging memory locations when an app starts, is disabled, or bypass ASLR altogether. The flaws could allow attackers to launch DoS attacks to make the server inaccessible to legitimate users, F5 explained. CVE-2026-93479 is similar, in that it is a map directive flaw that could allow attackers to send crafted HTTP requests to cause a heap buffer overflow; they can also execute code when ASLR is disabled, or bypass it. These vulnerabilities follow F5’s disclosure of CVE-2026-42530 in June. The flaw in ngx_http_v3_module in NGINX Open Source could also potentially allow remote attackers to cause DoS or trigger code execution. Customers can mitigate CVE-2026-15176 by avoiding use of the $request_filename variable and the alias directive in a location block, F5 said, and CVE-2026-97205 can be mitigated by disabling asynchronous file I/O (AIO) and Server Side Includes (SSI). Meanwhile, F5 advised mitigating CVE-2026-93479 by avoiding unnamed captures and instead using named captures and limiting their usage to the block with the regex match. But, noted Seva Ioussoufovitch , senior research analyst at Infotech, “since NGINX is used across a wide swath of systems, this may increase the risk of service availability loss for many enterprises.” The latest in a series of cybersecurity issues While these three vulnerabilities are not known to be exploited in the wild, F5 has repeatedly borne the brunt of cyberattacks in recent years, which is troubling because the cybersecurity and app delivery networking (ADN) company serves tens of thousands of customers, including 80% of the Fortune 500, analysts noted. Threat actors have repeatedly targeted flaws in its systems and products to map internal servers, hijack devices, breach systems, steal sensitive documents, and deploy data-wiping malware . Over the last five years, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged eight actively-exploited F5 vulnerabilities; four of these have been targeted in ransomware attacks . For instance, a 2025 nation-state breach and CISA’s Emergency Directive 26-01 centered on F5’s BIG-IP, and F5 said at the time that NGINX source code was not accessed. But, Dickson noted, NGINX’s own “warning shot” came in May when CVE-2026-42945 , a rewrite module overflow nicknamed NGINX Rift, arrived with a public remote code execution proof of concept. “This week’s alias and rewrite flaw lives in the same neighborhood,” he said, pointing out, “attackers read changelogs, too.” Mitigation Ioussoufovitch noted that the flaws are configuration-dependent, so enterprises should begin with an audit of current NGINX configurations to help risk-prioritize this patch. F5 also said that the risk of remote code execution (RCE) notably increases when ASLR is disabled, so users should double-check that ASLR and other typical OS-level protections are proactively enabled to at least limit the exploitation risk from similar types of attack. Enterprises need to ensure they have a clear inventory of which of their systems are running NGINX, including those where it is embedded in other products. This is critical to supporting configuration audits, segmentation efforts, and NGINX worker monitoring efforts, which can indicate that attackers “are poking at these types of vulnerabilities,” Ioussoufovitch said. “NGINX has already had multiple security releases this year, and I expect the trend to continue well into the future,” he noted. Dickson agreed that inventorying is the first step. NGINX “hides inside” ingress controllers, appliances, and container images. Many teams get NGINX from their Linux distribution, not nginx.org, and Amazon Linux still lists the AIO fix as pending. “A fix on the vendor’s site does not patch your servers,” he cautioned. As well as performing the inventory, enterprises should search their configurations for aliases paired with rewrite, AIO paired with SSI, and map blocks using unnamed regex captures. If an organization cannot patch today, the workarounds are simple, Dickson said: Disable AIO or stop serving SSI pages; switch map to named captures; confirm ASLR is on, run workers unprivileged; and segment the front door so it cannot reach the crown jewels. And, watch for worker processes that keep restarting. “These flaws need the right configuration to bite, and that is the good news,” Dickson said. “The bad news is that many organizations may not know what their NGINX configurations actually say.”
summary: F5 is once again disclosing cybersecurity flaws in its core offerings. The app delivery and security provider has released out-of-band (OOB) security patches that address multiple flaws in NGINX, its high-performance software that controls digital traffic for websites. These include three critical-severity flaws that could allow attackers to crash systems, execute code, and launch denial of service (DoS) attacks. OOB security patches are emergency software updates released outside of normal maintenance cycles.

title: Microsoft, Nvidia push provenance checks as open-weight AI adoption accelerates
raw_text: Microsoft and Nvidia are urging enterprises to assess the security of open-weight AI models throughout deployment, warning that changes to model weights and configurations can weaken safeguards even when a model retains its ability to perform assigned tasks. In a joint paper published last week, the companies identified 30 risk types across five categories and outlined a process for evaluating, mitigating, and monitoring them. The guidance calls for enterprises to verify model provenance, test the configurations they intend to deploy, and reassess risks after material changes. “Weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk,” the paper said . “Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards.” The framework covers cybersecurity, data protection, content, human-AI interaction, and bias. Its cybersecurity category includes malicious code generation, malicious tool calls, extraction of the model’s safety policies, excessive token generation, and behavior that diverges from the intended system goal. The paper draws on existing NIST and ISO risk-management standards and is the first in a planned series on managing risks across open-weight AI deployments, the companies said in a blog post. Model changes can weaken safeguards Open-weight models can be fine-tuned, merged with other models, modified, or repackaged for different uses. But those changes can weaken a model’s safety protections even when it continues to perform its intended task well, Microsoft and Nvidia said. “Safety behaviors are often the more fragile of the two,” the companies wrote. Changes to model weights, fine-tuning, quantization and configuration can “degrade safeguards while leaving task performance intact.” That creates a challenge for enterprise security teams: a model may continue to deliver accurate results on routine tasks even after changes have affected how it responds to unsafe requests. The companies advise enterprises to assess safety and capability separately, test the specific model configuration they intend to deploy, and repeat evaluations after significant changes. “No volume of behavioral testing establishes what an artifact is, only how it behaves,” the paper said. It recommends using cryptographic signatures to verify that a model matches the publisher’s original artifact. “Where signatures are unavailable, record the unverified integrity as an open risk rather than treating evaluation results as closing it,” the paper recommended. For enterprises, Gartner recommends independent adversarial testing, static scanning of model files, and provenance verification before and after deployment. Gartner’s proposed vetting process also calls for verifying model sources, checking file integrity, conducting adversarial testing, and recording approved models in an enterprise registry. Security must extend beyond the model Microsoft and Nvidia caution that evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of the application built around it. “Model evaluation alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application; enterprises must also assess permissions, data access, connected tools, runtime behavior, and operational controls,” the paper says. The guidance recommends assessing models in their intended operating context and maintaining controls across the model, runtime, harness, and application layers. It also calls for monitoring model inputs, outputs, and tool use after deployment. According to Gartner, open-weight model traffic must be routed through governed AI gateways to enforce authentication, prompt-injection defenses, sensitive-data protection and audit logging. The research firm also recommends isolating self-hosted runtimes and applying controls suited to other deployment models, including private network paths and customer-managed encryption keys for cloud API consumption. Gartner reported that client inquiries about open-weight models through its research inquiry service rose by more than 30% in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the first quarter. The firm projects that open-weight models will account for 50% of enterprise AI use cases by 2028, up from 20% at the time of its report. Staffing and accountability matter Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said self-hosting requires enterprises to account for the people and processes needed to maintain safeguards. “Self-hosting is a staffing decision as much as an infrastructure one, and the people to carry it must move with the model,” Gogia said. He cautioned against assuming that self-hosting necessarily means replacing all the safeguards available through managed services. In his assessment, a significant gap can be the provider’s misuse-investigation function, while customer responsibilities depend on the service and its configuration. Gogia said the Microsoft-Nvidia paper provides useful guidance but leaves important areas for future work. The authors say subsequent publications will extend risk-management guidance across the runtime, harness, and application layers. “The sharper question is who is contractually obliged to re-test and patch the model when a new stripping technique lands,” Gogia said. For CISOs, Gogia recommends assessing the model, deployment, and intended use before approving production workloads. He also advises security teams to retain control of their risk registers rather than relying exclusively on a vendor-developed taxonomy.
summary: Microsoft and Nvidia are urging enterprises to assess the security of open-weight AI models throughout deployment, warning that changes to model weights and configurations can weaken safeguards even when a model retains its ability to perform assigned tasks. In a joint paper published last week, the companies identified 30 risk types across five categories and outlined a process for evaluating, mitigating, and monitoring them. The guidance calls for enterprises to verify model provenance, test the configurations they intend to deploy, and reassess risks after material changes. “Weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk,” the paper said .

title: UK government adapts Post Office scandal redress schemes and investigates pre-Horizon software
raw_text:
The UK government has launched an investigation into software used by subpostmasters before the controversial Horizon system was rolled out, and has opened up new routes to compensation for scandal victims.

Despite compensation of over £1.7bn being paid to more than 14,000 victims of the Post Office scandal in Horizon redress schemes, there are claims of remaining unfairness and people being left out.

Furthermore, the government is launching a new investigation into pre-Horizon software and the impact of its errors. This includes the Capture system, which, like Horizon, led to unexplained losses and destroyed lives, including subpostmasters being convicted of crimes based on its data.

“To ensure no stone is left unturned in uncovering the full extent of issues affecting subpostmasters, a new independent investigation into software used before Horizon has also now been confirmed,” the government said.

There has already been an independent investigation into Capture by forensic experts at Kroll, which found there was a “reasonable likelihood” the Post Office software had caused accounting losses, but a new investigation could look deeper at the problems it caused.

Other systems such as ECCO+ have been pointed to as error-prone and likely to cause unexplained shortfalls that subpostmasters were forced to pay for, but beyond Computer Weekly investigations and work by campaigner Rupert Lloyds Thomas and the National Federation of Subpostmasters, little has been done to support affected users.

Read more about the Post Office’s ECCO+ software

  • Federation requests government investigation into third Post Office branch system.
  • Government looking into third faulty Post Office IT system.
  • Post Office Capture and Ecco+ users asked to make contact with Scottish statutory body.
  • Minister asks for evidence of Post Office ECCO+ system problems.
  • Email from 1999 reveals Post Office ECCO+ system crash problems.
  • Post Office acknowledges ECCO+ user’s calls for help three decades ago.

    New redress paths

    On financial redress, the government said it has introduced “a new package of measures to provide pathways to conclusion for schemes, strengthen scrutiny and fairness, and investigate pre-Horizon software”.

    New deadlines have been set for applications to a scheme for former users of the Post Office’s Capture system, which will now close on 31 March 2027, and a redress scheme for those wrongly convicted of crimes based on evidence from Horizon, which will close to new submissions on 27 July 2027.

    Over £9m has so far been paid to claimants through the Capture redress scheme, but claimants believe the sums they received fall well short. Earlier this month, Computer Weekly revealed that the husband of a former subpostmaster and Capture user, who had her financial and mental health destroyed at the hands of the Post Office, is preparing a judicial review to challenge the government’s financial redress decision.

    Ken Tooby warned the government that he will apply for judicial review of the decision to award him less than a third of a claim submitted on behalf of his late wife, June Tooby, who was blamed for losses recorded on the organisation’s faulty Capture software.

    As reported previously by Computer Weekly, another former subpostmaster, Lee Bowerman, received a financial settlement offer through the Capture redress scheme that equated to just 7% of his professionally calculated claim.

    Bowerman, who lost his business in South Wales more than 30 years ago, was part of a group that helped the government design the scheme.

    He complained that consequential losses were not included in the offer and that there was limited opportunity to appeal decisions on redress awards. He called for parity with former Horizon users, who were also affected in the Post Office scandal.

    The Horizon Shortfalls Scheme (HSS) is also being changed, with a new independent review process being introduced for subpostmasters who were previously told that there is insufficient evidence to receive a fixed sum offer of compensation.

    A new independent review process will also open next month for people who accepted HSS fixed sum offers and believe their claims were undervalued. 

    Following the latest government announcement, Post Office minister Kate Dearden said: “We must never lose sight of the suffering caused by the Horizon and Capture scandals. Behind every pound of compensation paid is a person whose life has been turned upside down by the scandal.

    “We remain unwavering in our commitment to provide fair, comprehensive and timely redress to all those affected and ensure that a scandal like this never happens again.” Registration remains open for the Horizon Family Members Redress Scheme, with claims processing expected to begin early next year. 

    The Post Office scandal was first exposed by Computer Weekly in 2009, revealing the stories of seven subpostmasters and the problems they suffered due to Horizon accounting software, which led to the most widespread miscarriage of justice in British history (see below timeline of Computer Weekly articles about the scandal since 2009).

The UK government has launched an investigation into software used by subpostmasters before the controversial Horizon system was rolled out, and has opened up new routes to compensation for scandal victims.

Despite compensation of over £1.7bn being paid to more than 14,000 victims of the Post Office scandal in Horizon redress schemes, there are claims of remaining unfairness and people being left out.

Furthermore, the government is launching a new investigation into pre-Horizon software and the impact of its errors. This includes the Capture system, which, like Horizon, led to unexplained losses and destroyed lives, including subpostmasters being convicted of crimes based on its data.

“To ensure no stone is left unturned in uncovering the full extent of issues affecting subpostmasters, a new independent investigation into software used before Horizon has also now been confirmed,” the government said.

There has already been an independent investigation into Capture by forensic experts at Kroll, which found there was a “reasonable likelihood” the Post Office software had caused accounting losses, but a new investigation could look deeper at the problems it caused.

Other systems such as ECCO+ have been pointed to as error-prone and likely to cause unexplained shortfalls that subpostmasters were forced to pay for, but beyond Computer Weekly investigations and work by campaigner Rupert Lloyds Thomas and the National Federation of Subpostmasters, little has been done to support affected users.

    On financial redress, the government said it has introduced “a new package of measures to provide pathways to conclusion for schemes, strengthen scrutiny and fairness, and investigate pre-Horizon software”.

    New deadlines have been set for applications to a scheme for former users of the Post Office’s Capture system, which will now close on 31 March 2027, and a redress scheme for those wrongly convicted of crimes based on evidence from Horizon, which will close to new submissions on 27 July 2027.

    Over £9m has so far been paid to claimants through the Capture redress scheme, but claimants believe the sums they received fall well short. Earlier this month, Computer Weekly revealed that the husband of a former subpostmaster and Capture user, who had her financial and mental health destroyed at the hands of the Post Office, is preparing a judicial review to challenge the government’s financial redress decision.

title: Capita postpones investor event to focus on CSPS fix
raw_text:
Capita cannot hold an event for shareholders, investors and market watchers because it wants to focus on fixing the botched administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS).

The troubled scheme has already reduced the firm’s profits by £40m.

The outsourcer said its Capital Market Event, planned for 4 November, had been postponed to enable it to “focus on improving the service delivery on the Civil Service Pension Scheme contract”.

It said it will include an update when it announces its trading statement next month. “Alongside its regular trading update in December, Capita will provide a comprehensive update, including detail on the group’s new operational segments following completion of the disposal of the private sector contact centre business,” said a company statement.

It added that it is making good operational progress with the CSPS contract. “This includes the roll-out of new features and further planned upgrades, such as the launch of the retirement modelling tool, which is due to go live in the coming weeks,” it said.

“Capita recognises further improvement in service is required, and we are implementing further automation and strengthening governance, including improved management information.”

Alongside the  Cabinet Office, it said it is working on a comprehensive recovery plan, “focusing on improving member experience and delivering operational stability”.

Pension disaster

In 2023, the Cabinet Office awarded Capita a seven-year contract worth £239m for the administration of the CSPS, which has 1.7 million members. The takeover from the previous administrator, MyCSP, took place on 1 December 2025. 

Since it took on the contract, Capita has failed to meet its delivery promises, leaving claimants in severe financial difficulties. Thousands of retired civil servants are affected by the CSPS problems – some have waited nearly a year for their pensions, and at least one has been forced to use a food bank.

Capita has admitted it is set to lose money on the contract, with pressure mounting on the organisation, which is heavily reliant on public sector business, due to the government’s current insourcing plans combined with its much-publicised failures.

In January 2026, just a month after Capita took over from MyCSP and following a litany of problems, a troubleshooter stepped in from HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) to lead an “urgent recovery plan”, which included 150 staff being moved temporarily from HMRC to the service.

Disaster after disaster has now prompted the government to make the decision to bring the service in-house, but no timeline has been given.

A Cabinet Office spokesperson recently told Computer Weekly that the government is “actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring the pension scheme back in-house” – a statement repeated by Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson.

What is now clear is that the government won’t let Capita flee without fixing a scheme it will inevitably lose. In the debate, Jameson declared her support for the government’s plan for the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, but made clear that Capita cannot just walk away, leaving a mess.

“I want Capita to pay for their mistakes, not the taxpayers to pay for their mistakes. They don’t get to just walk away and do nothing about it,” she told MPs. “They need to pay for this, they need to get everyone their pensions, and then we’ll look at what needs to be done in terms of the viability of the scheme long term.”

Civil servant campaign groups are demanding the scheme is fixed before the government makes a decision about its future.

title: ClickFix scams pose growing risk to education sector, Jisc says
raw_text:
As the Fresher’s Week hangovers fade and students across country turn their focus to the new academic year, so-called ClickFix social engineering scams targeting Britain’s higher education sector are kicking into high gear, according to academic IT and network services provider Jisc.

Amid the customary annual surge in phishing expeditions, Jisc said it is tracking a large number of ClickFix scams through its security operations sector (SOC) and cyber security incident response team (CSIRT)

ClickFix scams work by convincing users to copy, paste and run a certain set of commands on their system, usually to address and resolve a supposed technical issue. In doing so, they in fact run malicious applications that give threat actors access to the underlying network.

The organisation claims it has blocked between 300 and 37,000 phishing attacks every week against British colleges, research bodies and universities since the start of the current academic year – many of these emails will have been the precursor to a ClickFix scam.

 “Cyber criminals are constantly innovating new ways to gain access to networks. All organisations should ensure that employees and students are aware of ClickFix scams, and that no legitimate Catcha or verification check will ask users to copy, paste and run commands,” said Jisc head of security intelligence and capability, Nicole Stewart.

According to recent Microsoft disclosures, ClickFix attack volumes spiked more than 20 times between December 2025 and May 2026, with malware payloads following 96% of the time. Between February and May of this year, ClickFix user-pasted command execution was observed on over a million unique devices.

Multiple threat actors are known to leverage the ClickFix technique, which has proved highly effective since it bypasses most technical security measures.

The most prolific proponents of ClickFix attacks use them to deliver infostealers, such as LummaStealer – in the education sector such tools would be used to target research data for exfiltration, potentially by nation-state actors.

However, other threat actors have been observed using ClickFix attacks to deliver remote access trojans (Rats) such as Xworm, AsyncRAT, NetSupport and SectopRAT for hands-on keyboard activity, loaders suh as Latrodectus and MintsLoader to deliver additional malware and payloads, and even rootkits to allow their users to establish long-term persistence.

Microsoft said it has seen 23-fold growth in ClickFix volumes between December 2025 and May 2026, with malware payloads following 96% of the time while between February and May of this year, ClickFix user-pasted command execution was observed on over a million unique devices.

Jisc noted that some ClickFix scams now also store their malicious payloads on blockchain smart contracts instead of the threat actors’ own servers, which makes it considerably harder

Some variants are now also able to exploit the WebRTC standard for browser-based video calls and peer-to-peer data transfers, opening up a new avenue of attack.

Meanwhile, according to Microsoft, artificial intelligence (AI) techniques are now being used to manufacture ClickFix lures at scale – one  2025 campaign spread ClickFix activation steps via AI videos on TikTok, some of which were viewed more than half a million times.

Next steps

For defenders, prioritising user awareness and equipping people with the knowledge to identify and ward off social engineering attacks should be the first and most effective line of defence.

In particular, users should be made aware that legitimate websites or update tools will never ask them to copy and run code through the clipboard themselves. Any such prompts should be treated with extreme caution and IT security teams notified for assistance.

This said, acknowledging that even the most security-conscious people make mistakes from time to time, there are some technical steps that security teams can take to reduce the likelihood of an attempted ClickFix attack becoming a full-blown incident.

As a first step, security teams should enable browser-layer security protections wherever possible, and clamp down on user access to the Windows Run dialogue, PowerShell, or other living-off-the-land binaries (LoLbins). Where possible, endpoint telemetry should also be monitored to detect any process creation events launched via the clipboard feature.

title: PAC warns that UKRI is not delivering value for money
raw_text:
The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) and UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) are spending £9.2bn of taxpayers’ money on UK innovation. But, according to a report from the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), they need to do more to get better value for taxpayers from the UK government’s investments in research and development, and to keep the UK at the global forefront of innovation.

While the PAC noted that BIST has recently changed its procurement approach to make it more likely that UK companies will supply some of the £400m worth of specialised artificial intelligence (AI) chips it plans to purchase, the authors of the report said that British companies still find it much harder than their US counterparts to obtain the capital investment they need to grow while remaining based in the UK.

The report criticised UKRI for taking too cautious an approach when dealing with intellectual property. UKRI aims to strike a balance with the design of its IP controls so as not to inhibit companies’ growth. The PAC said that the more liberal approach to IP controls taken by UKRI, compared to other parts of the public sector, does not go far enough and BIST should go further to recover taxpayers’ money. The PAC suggest UKRI could, for example, look to take more equity stakes where it is providing funding.

Geoffrey Clifton-Brown MP, chair of the Public Accounts Committee, said: “It may strike followers of this committee’s work that our call for government to take a less cautious approach to taking a direct stake in British innovation is an unusual one. But we are a body dedicated to value for taxpayers’ money, not hoarding it. The nations currently leading the global tech race did not achieve their positions by avoiding more entrepreneurial policies. This is a simple case for the government of nothing ventured, nothing gained.”

The PAC was also critical of UKRI’s approach to cancelling projects it had already funded. In the report, the PAC said that UKRI cancelled funding for its airborne laboratory five years after deciding to upgrade it, having spent £46m of the £49m budget.

“We believe it could have taken action sooner. UKRI could also have been quicker to realise the Science and Facilities Technology Council’s (STFC’s) plans were unaffordable,” the report’s authors said. “The decisions it will soon take to bring spending back under control could have serious consequences for the UK’s skills base, for sites such as the Daresbury research campus, and for the UK’s reputation as a partner in international collaborations such as CERN.”

Another area of concern raised by the PAC is UKRI’s ability to maintain and upgrade infrastructure needed to support research. It reported that restoring university-owned research infrastructure to a fully operational condition would cost £5.6bn, at a time when many universities have large financial deficits. 

In the report, the PAC noted that BIST and UKRI failed to ensure the Archer2 national supercomputer’s replacement would be ready before Archer2 is turned off. The PAC said the 13-month expected delay would have been longer without the University of Edinburgh’s decision to proactively prepare its site by upgrading a grid connection.

Looking at regional differences, the PAC found that the current VAT framework for research infrastructure, along with other barriers, discourages researchers from using facilities outside their own institution.

“We also heard that UKRI has focused on large investments and paid less attention to whether the overall landscape is balanced, efficient and resilient,” it noted.

Clifton-Brown added: “Our report also identifies a continuing and unacceptable regional divide in researchers’ experiences outside of London and the South East. UKRI’s spending in the North seems to be going in the right direction, but without a dedicated focus on rebalancing the scales, there is every possibility of slipping back to the previous status quo.”

title: Google Cloud power event knocks out UK banks, courts and couriers
raw_text:
A power problem in Google Cloud’s London region knocked out banking apps, the courts’ video platform and delivery networks across the UK on Tuesday 20 October, with no second Google UK region for customers to fall back on.

By late afternoon, most services had recovered. Google said the issue affected only a “very small number” of customers, while the Ministry of Justice confirmed the courts’ Cloud Video Platform had still not fully recovered. Google said: “We will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our internal investigation.”

The outage began just after 7.00am BST when the europe-west2-b availability zone – one of three inside Google’s London region, europe-west2 – lost power. Google Cloud confirmed the cause: “A power event caused an outage within europe-west2-b zone. The power event is mitigated. We are seeing the recovery of services and are prioritising the recovery of existing workloads.”

The incident is the latest reminder that the UK’s largest businesses remain dangerously exposed to cloud outages. Because europe-west2 is Google’s only UK region, customers that had not built multi-region resilience had no second UK location to failover to.

The failure hit four Google Cloud locations:

  1. europe-west2 (London) – Google’s only UK region, where the failure struck.
  2. europe-west2-b – the availability zone that lost power.
  3. europe-west2-a and europe-west2-c – the peer zones that, by one engineer’s account, did not fully absorb the load.
  4. europe-north2 – one administrator also reported VPC, Cloud NAT and load-balancer issues here.

For UK customers, the outage rippled through a long list of household names:

  • Banks and fintech: Revolut, Lloyds Bank, HSBC, Barclays, Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Halifax, Nationwide, Emma and credit-reference firm Equifax.
  • Delivery and retail: Royal Mail, DPD and Screwfix.
  • Property and web services: Rightmove, BT and hosting firm SiteGround.
  • Public sector: NHS England, HM Courts & Tribunals Service and Gov.uk.

The day unfolded like this:

  • 07.05 – VPC, Cloud NAT and load-balancer issues began in europe-west2, with one administrator also reporting europe-north2.
  • 10.00 – The courts’ Cloud Video Platform went down across large parts of England and Wales.
  • 10.57 – Google confirmed “an issue with multiple services in europe-west2”.
  • 11.03 – DownDetector logged thousands of reports across Google, Revolut, Lloyds, HSBC, Barclays, Halifax, Royal Mail, Bank of Scotland, DPD and Sky.
  • 11.05 – Revolut told customers that “all our customers’ money and data are safe”.
  • 11.16 – NHS England, HM Courts & Tribunals Service and Gov.uk appeared to be affected.
  • 11.27 – The Criminal Bar Association warned that trials and hearings “can not proceed”.
  • 12.27 – Google said the power event was mitigated and partial mitigation would follow within 30 minutes.
  • 12.45 – The first administrators reported virtual machines in europe-west2-b rebooted and services restored.
  • 14.48 – Google reported “recovery of services for most workloads in europe-west2”.
  • 14.59 – UK Power Networks confirmed its London systems ran normally, ruling out a substation fault.
  • 15.10 – Google said only a “very small number” of customers remained affected.
  • 15.52 – The Ministry of Justice confirmed its systems were not yet fully restored.

The failure also played out in real time on Reddit among the IT professionals who had to manage it. One engineer posting as Rs3_Myway, who said they were “on calls at work dealing with it”, wrote: “Availability zone B went down with power cut. A and C, for some reason, didn’t pick up the slack completely in prod (unclear why). Apigee gateway as the big problem system.”

An administrator relaying Google’s engineering update described the root cause: “Although mains power has returned, backup generators failed to engage during the initial outage. As a result, Engineering is maintaining a frontend and backend drain on the europe-west2-b clusters while onsite technicians verify backend power functionality.”

Another user summed up the structural problem: “It is the only Google region in the UK so businesses/banks/NHS etc. here can’t switch to another location.”

And an IT manager posting as Crimsondelo reported the fallout across their own supply chain: “We are seeing outages on several of our providers including Equifax. Apparently Lloyds is having issues as well.”

The episode echoes an Amazon Web Services outage that knocked out UK tax office and banking services last autumn, and it lands as investment banks lose £600,000 an hour to IT failures. For enterprise buyers, the lesson is architectural – a single-zone service in a single-region footprint remains a single point of failure, and data sovereignty does little to help when the only region available is the one that went down.

title: AstraZeneca works with Oracle to speed up drug trials
raw_text:
AstraZeneca is working with Oracle to investigate the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and real-world data to help identify eligible patients for clinical trials. The two companies also plan to accelerate evidence generation, and bring relevant research insights into everyday care using Oracle’s health data, cloud, AI, analytics and clinical workflow capabilities.

Pascal Soriot, AstraZeneca CEO, described the collaboration as “unique”. “Combining AstraZeneca’s world-class science with Oracle’s deep data and technology expertise, we can help clinicians identify patients sooner, optimise clinical trials, and generate evidence continuously across the lifecycle of a medicine,” he said.

Anne-Claire Gerbaldi, chief digital, data and AI officer at AstraZeneca, said the use of AI to improve clinical trials is the next evolution of medicine. “Too many patients are diagnosed late or face a long journey to get the care they need,” she said. “To build the next decade of medicine, we aim to harness AI to connect learnings across science, clinical trials and everyday care, generating insights that continuously strengthen research, accelerate innovation and enhance patient outcomes.”

Through a non-binding agreement, the companies plan to explore selected use cases that could improve clinical trial efficiency and success by leveraging modern applications and AI to help care teams identify eligible patients earlier and easier, resulting in greater access to clinical trials for patients in need and helping to overcome one of the largest obstacles in clinical trials – patient recruitment. Disease areas the two companies are looking to explore include oncology; cardiovascular, renal and metabolic diseases; respiratory and immunology; and rare disease.

The collaboration is international and involves working with governments. Oracle and AstraZeneca plan to start with a focus on supporting hypertension care and clinical research in Abu Dhabi, in partnership with healthcare company M42. According to AstraZeneca, this will help clinical teams identify patients with uncontrolled hypertension; implementing guideline-directed care; and improving the recruitment for clinical trials.

“Some of the most important opportunities for AI are in healthcare, where better use of data can help turn scientific innovation into better outcomes for patients,” said Mike Sicilia, Oracle CEO.

“By bringing AstraZeneca’s scientific expertise together with Oracle’s data, cloud, AI and healthcare capabilities, we have an opportunity to help accelerate research, connect more patients to clinical trials, and ultimately bring relevant insights into care faster.”

The collaboration with Oracle comes just a few days after AstraZeneca announced it had entered into a new strategic drug discovery collaboration and licensing agreement with Insitro, an AI therapeutics company.

AstraZeneca said the collaboration will see advanced AI systems being deployed to identify novel drug targets using Insitro’s Virtual Human AI platform. This brings together large-scale human and cellular data with AI-enabled target identification and medicine design, generating insights to inform the discovery of novel therapeutic candidates.

Sharon Barr, executive vice-president and head of BioPharmaceuticals R&D at AstraZeneca, said: “We know that disease biology is incredibly complex, and one of the most critical decisions in R&D is selecting the right target. This strategic collaboration underscores our commitment to maximising the potential of cutting-edge AI to tackle the root cause of disease. Partnering with Insitro, we will use advanced AI to identify the biological drivers of disease to support the rapid discovery of high-quality novel targets, advancing our ambition to deliver the next generation of medicines to patients faster.”

title: FCA gets hundreds of applicants for two top artificial intelligence roles
raw_text:
The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has received hundreds of applications for two senior roles specialising in artificial intelligence (AI) and data science.

The advertised roles are for a head of agentic AI and data science research and a head of department, with salaries of between £126,000 and £190,000 per year.

According to a Bloomberg report, Jessica Rusu, the FCA’s chief information and AI officer, confirmed it has received hundreds of applicants for the two jobs.

She told Bloomberg: “We have two senior leadership roles in the market now and we have had hundreds of really high-quality applications.”

Both roles are now closed to applications.

Passion for AI and doing the right thing

One senior banking IT professional, who wished to remain anonymous, said the people applying for these jobs are in it for the “mission” rather than the money, which he said is less than they could earn in the private sector.

“I think these jobs appeal to people who truly are passionate about what happens to AI, regardless of what they get paid. I think there would be a queue of people who are not so worried about the pay,” he added. “They’re more interested in getting AI under control and getting it regulated and keeping a close eye on it.”

In July, a “landmark review” by the FCA described AI as a “defining force” that will change financial services for consumers, but one that could “amplify risks”.

The regulator’s push for the right advanced tech skills to help it combat increased tech-based threats and use tech to better regulate has been going on for half a decade.

FCA CEO Nikhil Rathi said last year that the regulator had “embraced data and technology to crack down on harm and ensure high standards”.

Building data and AI expertise

In 2022, as part of a “heavy” investment in data, the FCA said it wanted to hire people with expertise in AI, analytics and data science, as well as cloud engineering and digital technology. This was in addition to the 100 people it had hired since 2020.

At the time, Rusu said: “Better use of data means we can be more proactive and find and stop harm faster. We are continuing to improve our data, technology and capabilities to act decisively in consumers’ interests, while making it easier for firms to report to us.” 

It opened a new digital delivery centre in Leeds that year, and announced plans to double the number of staff in its Edinburgh office to around 200 and increase recruitment in data and technology. 

Rusu told a Bloomberg event in London that the FCA is building AI tools to help oversee anti-money laundering controls at 60,000 extra firms to meet new rules that come in 2028. She said it is also using AI agents to help supervise thousands of small firms that report wholesale market transactions.

Beyond using AI to regulate, the FCA wants to firm up defences against cyber security risks and potential fraud emanating from the technology.

“AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed,” said Rusu. “That means regulators will increasingly need to make judgements without precedent, while ensuring that trust remains at the heart of financial services.”

title: Teachers’ pension transfers from Capita on eve of government’s civil service scheme decision
raw_text:
The switchover of the teachers’ pension scheme from Capita to Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), which begins this week, will be closely watched as government faces decision time over Capita’s failed civil service pension administration.

If all goes to plan, a blackout on the teachers’ pension website is planned from 22 October to 2 November, when the scheme completes its transfer to Indian IT giant TCS.

Capita has run the service for more than 20 years, but TCS secured a 10-year Department for Education contract in 2023, the same year Capita won the contract to take over the civil service pension scheme (CSPS), which since its go live has been a monumental disaster (see box below).

It won’t just be teachers braced for the transfer of more than two million pension accounts from Capita to TCS, but also the government, which is under pressure to strip Capita of the CSPS. It has already removed the outsourcing firm from the contract to administer the Royal Mail pension scheme, following failure to meet key milestones, and is still to decide the scheme’s future administration delivery.

Pension problems

As Computer Weekly revealed earlier this month, MPs heard that some teachers are experiencing problems with their pensions. In light of Capita’s disastrous takeover of the Civil Service Pension Scheme, a Westminster Hall debate was held, where MPs discussed the botched scheme.

During the packed-out meeting, Alison Bennet, Liberal Democrat MP for Mid Sussex, said she had been told teachers were experiencing problems with their pensions. She asked: “Are we seeing teachers go through the same ordeal [as civil servants]?

“I have received very concerning casework from teachers in my constituency who seem to be having similar or the same troubles with their pensions,” added Bennet. “The idea that the immense stress and potential financial hardship we’ve heard inflicted on civil servants has been [repeated] with teachers is appalling.”

One former teacher who is supporting teachers with concerns told Computer Weekly earlier this month that there are thousands of anomalies in the data being transferred that could see teachers lose out. “I have been encouraging teachers to make copies of the data that they have available through the website,” he said.

A Department for Education spokesperson repeated an earlier statement that the scheme has some “clearly unacceptable” delays. The spokesperson said it expects Capita to “closely with those affected … resolve issues as quickly as possible and keep them informed throughout”.

The government department confirmed the transfer will be complete on 1 November, with the website and member/employer portal available from 2 November.

TCS and Capita were contacted for an update on progress but had not responded when this article was published.

Decision time

The government is currently deciding what to do with the CSPS and Royal Mail schemes. It’s Strategic Review of Pension Scheme Delivery is at its “discovery phase”, where it is considering a range of options, including insourcing and increased digital delivery for the schemes.

In a recent briefing to members, PCS general secretary Fran Heathcote said the government hopes to develop its “strategic position” by next month. A decision, if made next month, will come soon after TCS’s teachers’ pension administration goes live.

Heathcote told union members that the government is considering the “feasibility of insourcing pension administration”, as well as “greater consistency and alignment across public service schemes, shared delivery approaches between schemes, future digital delivery options, and the practical implications of major organisational change”.

The PCS’s Heathcote also said the National Trade Union Congress has highlighted government ambitions to strengthen internal digital capability and said the review should examine: “The feasibility of an in-house digital pension platform. The timescales required to develop such a system. Alternative suppliers if an internal solution is not viable.”

TCS’s takeover of the teachers’ pension scheme, which involves digitally transforming it, will give the government a live case to watch closely.

Botched AI project

Capita had planned a similar transformation with the CSPS but its grand plan to use artificial intelligence (AI) to revolutionise pension scheme delivery failed when the tech didn’t work.

Simon Hoare MP, who chairs the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee, said during a select committee hearing about the CSPS failures: “The Cabinet Office was told that the two-year transition period would lead to the digital artificial intelligence revolution to deliver a world-class, world-leading pension service. None of that met neither the novel nor the basic.”

Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez conceded: “We have not been able to deploy the technology that would allow us to get there.”

What resulted is becoming a scandal as retired civil servants and the families of deceased scheme members have been left without the funds they are owed – for nearly a year in some cases – due to Capta’s mistakes.

title: CIOs admit they are being forced to upgrade enterprise IT
raw_text:
A Censuswide survey of 2,018 CIOs and senior IT decision-makers at large organisations in the US and UK for independent software maintenance provider Origina has found that organisations spend almost $13m on upgrades pushed by IT providers.

On average, 28% of enterprise software budgets go on upgrades, migrations and licensing changes driven by their IT suppliers. IT leaders who took part in the study reported that their organisation would not have actively chosen to upgrade.

This has a profound effect on new projects, which extends to artificial intelligence (AI) initiatives. Asked about the last time an AI or data programme was slowed, paused or cancelled, 34% said IT supplier-driven costs made a major contribution to that decision, and a further 56% a moderate one.

The research published in Origina’s The software tax report, in partnership with Thinkers50, suggests these costs have shifted the balance of power between buyers and sellers. Customers exercise choice once, at the point of purchase. After that, control over the timing and terms of change passes largely to the IT supplier.

Out of those surveyed, 78% agree their primary provider of enterprise software, rather than their own organisation, sets the timing and terms of change. A similar proportion said they would have no meaningful choice but to accept if a major enterprise IT provider changed its commercial terms. Some 76% said their organisation has very little real leverage in negotiations, and 80% said moving away from major IT suppliers would cause significant disruption.

While software as a service (SaaS) and cloud computing make deployment, updates, access and security simpler, the report’s authors said that the shift from owning software to renting access also changed the economic relationship.

“Switching off a service became easier technically; switching away from the provider could become harder commercially and operationally,” they warned. “Over several decades, dependence accumulated with few external guardrails to constrain it.”

Marshall Van Alstyne, professor at Boston University and co-author of The software tax, said: “Economists have studied this problem for decades: once a customer makes relationship-specific investments, the vendor gains leverage that no contract can fully anticipate.

“For CIOs, the lesson is simple: negotiate the exit before the entry. You don’t have to leave a vendor to benefit from being able to.”

The report points out that an organisation can rationally accept an unfavourable upgrade if refusing it means losing support, creating a security risk or jeopardising access to software on which critical operations depend.

“What looks irrational when the upgrade is considered in isolation may be perfectly rational when the available alternatives are considered alongside it,” the report’s authors said. “The customers in this survey had a choice, but by the time it had to be made, their realistic options had already narrowed.”

Tomás O’Leary, CEO and founder of Origina and co-author of The Software Tax, said: “When the alternative to an unwanted upgrade is losing support on systems the business runs on, saying yes is often a rational response.

“That’s exactly the problem. The market has left some of the most experienced technology leaders in the world with little room to refuse, and that cost shows up in budgets, in engineering time and in innovation that never gets funded. We want to make that cost visible so customers can start to take back control of it.”

title: Keep less, know more: the AI advantage hiding in your data estate
raw_text:
Most organisations are preparing for AI by consolidating and retaining more data. But the stronger strategy is arguably the opposite. One of the most valuable ways to prepare for enterprise AI this year is actually to dispose of data. This runs counter to a decade of data strategy built around consolidation and the assumption that more data automatically delivers better outcomes. But doing a bit of housekeeping is, in fact, a fast route to a more effective AI roll-out and more defensible General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) position.

The estate your assistant will actually read

Data estates drift by accident rather than by design. Consider the SharePoint site a team set up in 2019 so an external contractor could reach a single document, which no one ever decommissioned. Or the four iterations of the expenses policy living on a server, three of them superseded, but none marked accordingly. Think of the shared drive left behind after a restructure that still contains a redundancy list, or an absence spreadsheet a former employee saved outside the HR system. The data had been protected simply because it was hard to find, although this was never an intentional security measure.

If you deploy an AI assistant that indexes everything on your systems, problems will inevitably arise at go-live. Personal data that should have been disposed of becomes trivially discoverable. When an AI assistant is presented with four versions of a policy and no indication of which is the most current, it is likely to answer from the wrong one with complete confidence.

Data minimisation, complimented by other key controls like role-based access control (RBAC), remain essential to ensure systems can only access information appropriate to a user's role and authority.

This isn’t just an IT headache, but a direct tax on AI efficacy, as the cost of inaction will hit performance. Gartner predicts that organisations that prioritise semantics in AI-ready data will increase their GenAI model accuracy by up to 80% and reduce costs by up to 60% by 2027, which shows the value of investment.

Dispose before you index

Most programmes plan to tackle these issues after the pilot phase. After all, few leaders are willing to fund a data clear-out for a capability that has yet to prove its value. However, the economics point the other way. A file deleted before it’s indexed is gone with just one click, whereas deleting it afterwards means removing it from the source repository, search indexes, cached embeddings, and potentially a model that will need retraining.

Sequencing therefore matters more than just the tooling. To fix this, it’s important to start looking at the data repositories that have no clear owner, which carry the highest ratio of risk to value, and apply a straightforward test to everything else. For example, if a document were quoted verbatim in a response to an employee next week, would that be acceptable? If the answer is no, it does not belong in scope, regardless of its speculative future value.

Ownership is the control most programmes lack

It’s always worth remembering that data becomes risky at the point that it becomes nobody’s responsibility. An employee leaves, their files remain, and often no one can say with confidence what they contain, whether they're still needed or whether they can be deleted. If you multiply that across a decade of turnover, it accounts for much of the exposure in most large organisations.

The answer is straightforward: every significant data set should have a named owner with the authority to make decisions about it. Not a committee or a lengthy approval process, but a person who can quickly decide whether an AI tool should have access to their part of the business. The most common cause of delay in AI approvals is not risk appetite, but the inability to establish who decides. Stripping away dead data and establishing this clear ownership is the exact mechanism that allows organisations to deploy AI further and faster than competitors bogged down in uncurated data swamps.

Purpose has to travel with the data

Purpose limitation is another area where these programmes often come unstuck. Information collected for one reason, such as payroll, can quietly become reference material for an assistant, simply because integration was easy. The safeguard is to attach purpose and lawful basis to the data itself, rather than burying them in a register that quickly falls out of date. Done properly, teams can see at a glance which datasets are suitable for a particular AI use case and which are not.

The instinct to consolidate everything into one repository deserves scrutiny. The European Data Protection Board’s draft guidelines on anonymisation, published in July, are clear that data stripped of identifiers remains personal data where it sits in a store that cannot be cleanly separated from records identifying individuals. Purpose-bound collections are easier to defend and easier to evaluate for accuracy.

The Computer Weekly Security Think Tank on GDPR and AI

  • Rik Ferguson, Forescout: AI has exposed the cracks GDPR was already trying to fix.
  • Javvad Malik, KnowBe4: When the intern has admin rights: GDPR in the agentic age.
  • Haris Pylarinos, Hack The Box: GDPR wasn't designed for AI and that's a security problem.

Provenance, and the expiry of assurance

Responding properly to an access or erasure request also means knowing where each record originated and which downstream copies exist. Teams have long treated provenance as an engineering refinement that can be addressed later. But it is often the difference between a response measured in hours and one measured in months. The risk is that you tell someone their data has gone, confirm it to the individual, and leave the assistant answering from a copy nobody tracked.

Assurance ages the same way. An impact assessment signed in March describes a system that by September carries a different model version, new data sources and an agent performing actions nobody reviewed. It’s important to give assessments review dates and version references, so the evidence describes the up-to-date system in production.

Restraint as competitive advantage

There is time to do this deliberately. The Digital Omnibus has moved the AI Act’s obligations for higher risk standalone systems to December 2027, and the ICO has confirmed a statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision making for 2026 and 2027. That interval creates value only if it is spent on the estate rather than on documentation about it.

The organisations that get furthest with AI will not be those holding the most information. They will be those able to state, for anything they hold, what it is for, who owns it, where it came from and when it goes. For years, data minimisation has been treated as a brake on progress. In reality, it is now becoming one of the reasons some organisations are able to move faster than others.

Dhairya Mehta is a data expert at PA Consulting
